text: Energy security vital to Việt Nam's double-digit growth ambitions

HCM CITY - Ensuring a stable and sustainable energy supply has become an urgent priority as Viet Nam targets average annual GDP growth of more than 10 per cent during 2026-30, requiring commercial electricity consumption to increase by around 11-12 per cent annually.

The issue was highlighted at the Sustainable Energy Development Forum held in HCM City on November 19 by the Việt Nam Chamber of Commerce and Industry (VCCI) and its Business Forum Magazine, bringing together policymakers, experts and businesses to discuss energy security and the transition towards a greener economy.
Addressing the event, Hoàng Quang Phòng, VCCI Vice Chairman, said global energy market volatility and climate-related challenges had underscored the importance of ensuring reliable energy supplies.

Although Việt Nam had maintained relatively stable supplies of electricity and petroleum products to support socio-economic development, risks remained, particularly its dependence on imported energy, limited petroleum reserves and delays in power generation and transmission projects.

Phòng said Việt Nam's commitment to achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 was creating pressure for businesses to transform production methods while opening up opportunities in green manufacturing, the circular economy and energy efficiency.

Companies in textiles and garments, construction and manufacturing had begun adopting rooftop solar power, new technologies and energy-saving solutions to reduce emissions and improve competitiveness.
However, businesses continued to face barriers, including high initial investment costs, lengthy payback periods, inconsistent policy frameworks and limited access to green financing.
Closer cooperation among regulators, businesses and investors was therefore needed to mobilise resources for a modern, safe and reliable energy system, he said.

Nguyễn Đức Hiển, deputy head of the Party Central Committee's Commission for Policies and Strategies, said electricity demand needed to increase by around 11-12 per cent annually to support the country's double-digit growth ambitions during 2026-30.
However, electricity generation in 2026 was projected to grow by approximately 10.3 per cent, below the level required.
Việt Nam's dependence on imported energy had risen from 8.4 per cent in 2015 to around 44 per cent in 2025, while its primary energy supply remained heavily reliant on fossil fuels.
Coal accounted for approximately 55 per cent, petroleum 26 per cent and natural gas 5 per cent, while renewable energy and electricity made up around 13 per cent.
One of the most pressing concerns was the slow implementation of power generation and transmission projects.
Without effective solutions, the electricity system could face a capacity shortfall of approximately 4,300MW in 2027, rising to 13,964MW by 2030.
LNG-fired power and offshore wind projects also faced difficulties relating to pricing mechanisms, power purchase agreements, minimum offtake commitments and investment risk-sharing arrangements.
Meanwhile, limited domestic capacity in equipment manufacturing and supporting industries continued to constrain local value creation in the energy supply chain.
Hiển called for the completion of financial mechanisms and power purchase agreements for LNG and offshore wind projects, alongside the development of shared LNG storage and port infrastructure.
He also stressed the need to resolve outstanding renewable energy projects, encourage private investment in electricity transmission and accelerate the development of a competitive energy market.
Direct power purchase agreements (DPPA), rooftop solar systems for self-consumption and green financing should also be promoted to diversify energy sources and mobilise investment, he said.

Bùi Quốc Hoan, deputy general director of the Southern Power Corporation (EVNSPC), said reliable electricity supplies were essential to economic development, particularly as southern localities sought to attract investment and expand industrial production.

EVNSPC was prioritising investment in electricity infrastructure and developing smart grids to improve reliability and facilitate the integration of renewable energy, particularly distributed power sources.
These systems would help strengthen energy security while supporting green growth, digital transformation and sustainable development across the southern region, he said.

Participants at the forum also discussed the development of green energy industries, legal frameworks for emerging energy sources, international experience in energy transition and the establishment of a national energy reserve strategy.
Phòng said Việt Nam needed a comprehensive approach combining institutional reform, infrastructure investment, technological innovation and stronger public-private partnerships.

Ensuring energy security was not only essential to maintaining macroeconomic stability but also a foundation for achieving high economic growth, strengthening national competitiveness and advancing sustainable development, he stressed. - VNS
